rows.Finding / value: Sushma Swaraj (14 February 1952–6 August 2019), lawyer, parliamentarian and BJP leader; born in Ambala, in present-day Haryana.

Studied at SD College and Panjab University; began Supreme Court practice in 1973. JP-movement participation and her self-described RSS-family/ABVP background provide distinct strands of political formation.
Moved from Haryana politics to both Houses of Parliament, Union ministries and a brief Delhi chief ministership; led the Lok Sabha opposition before becoming External Affairs Minister.
Contested for Janata in 1977 and 1980, and for BJP by 1984. Her own account links an RSS family, student activism and socialist connections; these are not interchangeable organizational memberships.
Eleven direct contests: seven victories and four defeats; three additional Rajya Sabha elections. Assembly: three wins. Lok Sabha: four wins and four losses.
Ambala Cantt and Karnal in Haryana; South Delhi and Hauz Khas; the 1999 Bellary challenge; Vidisha in 2009 and 2014. Rajya Sabha service also provided a route back to national office.

First woman Chief Minister of Delhi and first woman Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha; first woman to hold External Affairs full time. The qualification matters: earlier women had held additional charge.

Documented interventions include film-finance access, tobacco legislation, consular evacuation coordination, grievance tracking and passport-document reform. Implementation and long-term effects require separate evidence.

Her record combines citizen-facing services with parliamentary and bilateral negotiation. The Bangladesh boundary measure and Pakistan dialogue agreement illustrate collective government diplomacy rather than sole authorship.
Major disputes concerned Lalit Modi’s travel papers and communication with families of Indians missing in Iraq. The workbook records criticism, her replies and the limits of procedural evidence.

Institutional firsts and accessible consular leadership are strong themes in remembrance. A balanced assessment also preserves partisan nationalism, controversies and limits on attributing government outcomes to one minister.
Career through her death in August 2019; selected posthumous recognition. Sources accessed 5 October 2026. Historical legal dispositions are dated, not asserted as current case-status updates.
